w: Before it was a museum, this was simply home: William Herschel's townhouse on New King Street, shared with his sister and fellow astronomer Caroline. It's been open to visitors since 1981, letting you stand in the rooms where two of the era's sharpest eyes on the night sky once lived and worked.
_facts: museum at 19 New King Street, Bath
inaugurated in 1981
formerly home of William Herschel and sister Caroline

w: Named for Sulis, the goddess of the hot spring the Romans found bubbling where the Fosse Way crosses the Avon: a walled temple and bath complex grew here by the 3rd century AD, then silted up for a thousand years. Elizabethans reopened the springs; 1900s excavators finally uncovered the Great Bath beneath it all.
s: Where Rome bathed in Sulis' sacred spring
_facts: Roman town established shortly after arrival in Britain
sits where Fosse Way crosses the River Avon, at hot springs
walled temple and bath complex by 3rd century AD, declined by 5th century
Great Bath excavated and given neo-classical superstructure by 1900s

w: One collector's obsession became a city's museum: Doris Langley Moore handed her costume collection to Bath in 1963, and it grew into more than 100,000 objects of fashionable dress - the earliest an embroidered shirt and gloves from around 1600. Housed in the Assembly Rooms, it still pulls in visitors by the thousand.
_facts: formerly Museum of Costume, housed in the Assembly Rooms
collection started by Doris Langley Moore, donated 1963
over 100,000 objects, late 16th century to present
earliest pieces c.1600 embroidered shirts and gloves

w: John Wood the Elder opened his grand Palladian sequence here in the early 18th century - Queen Square, then the Circus, then the Royal Crescent - sub-letting plots to builders who kept his facade intact. Beau Nash raised an obelisk here in 1738 for Frederick, Prince of Wales; bombs hit the south side in the Bath Blitz.
s: Where Bath's Georgian grand plan began
_facts: first element of Bath's key architectural sequence with the Circus and Royal Crescent
designed by John Wood the Elder, early 18th century, Palladian style
obelisk erected by Beau Nash in 1738 for Frederick, Prince of Wales
south side bombed in WWII Bath Blitz, later restored

w: Alexander Pope and Capability Brown shaped this valley south of Bath for Ralph Allen in the 1720s, defining the 'English landscape garden' style later copied across Europe. A Palladian bridge crosses the lake below Allen's mansion, later a Catholic school; the National Trust restored the grounds in the 1990s.
s: Pope and Capability Brown's valley garden
_facts: designed 18th century by Alexander Pope and Capability Brown
influential in defining the English landscape garden style
bought by Ralph Allen in 1720s
National Trust acquired and restored it in the 1990s
features a Palladian bridge and lake

w: The only UK museum built solely around East and Southeast Asian art: a retired Hong Kong solicitor, Brian McElney, spent decades collecting ceramics, jade, bronzes and bamboo carvings, then handed it all to Bath. Nearly 2,000 objects now fill a restored Georgian townhouse, spanning from 5000 BCE to the present day.
s: A Hong Kong solicitor's Asian art trove
_facts: only UK museum dedicated solely to East and Southeast Asian art
collection from Brian McElney, retired Hong Kong solicitor
almost 2,000 objects, 5000 BCE to present
housed in a restored Georgian townhouse

w: Bath's first public art gallery began as one man's collection: Sir William Holburne's fine and decorative arts, works by Gainsborough, Stubbs and Zoffany, housed at the edge of Sydney Pleasure Gardens. A 2011 extension by Eric Parry Architects, Heritage Lottery funded, gave it a cafe spilling into the gardens.
_facts: Bath's first public art gallery, Grade I listed
built around Sir William Holburne's collection
artists include Gainsborough, Guardi, Stubbs, Ramsay, Zoffany
reopened 2011 after Eric Parry Architects extension, Heritage Lottery funded

w: William Beckford - novelist and art collector, one of Georgian England's richest men - built this neo-classical folly on Lansdown Hill in 1827 as a private library and retreat, reached via a landscaped walk called Beckford's Ride. After his death it became a chapel and cemetery; a 1931 fire nearly finished it off.
s: An eccentric's neo-classical folly on a hill
_facts: architectural folly built 1827 for William Beckford, novelist and collector
designed by Henry Goodridge, on Lansdown Hill
used as library and retreat with belvedere cupola
became burial ground/chapel after Beckford's death 1844
damaged by fire 1931; restored by Bath Preservation Trust after 1993 purchase
